name: FEMA flood zone (FLD_ZONE)
plain: The letter code that the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) gives a mapped flood area. A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE mean a 1% yearly chance of flooding (VE adds storm waves on the coast), and X and D mean lower or unstudied hazard.
definition: FLD_ZONE is the flood zone code of one map shape (polygon) in the National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). The NFHL is the digital version of FEMA's flood insurance rate maps. In the 2026-10 snapshot, this file holds eight codes for Puerto Rico: A, A99, AE, AH, AO, VE, X and D. Zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE form the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA): land FEMA maps with a 1% chance of flooding in any year (the '100-year flood'). Zone X has two parts, told apart by the ZONE_SUBTY field: a shaded 0.2% part (the '500-year flood') and an unshaded part of minimal hazard.
geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

method: The build downloads layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones) of the NFHL for every record whose DFIRM_ID (the identifier of FEMA's Digital Flood Insurance Rate Map database) starts with 72, the Puerto Rico code. It publishes FLD_ZONE, ZONE_SUBTY and SFHA_TF. Outlines are simplified to about 5 m (0.00005 degrees) for display, and no polygon is dropped. The map layer draws the SFHA zones and zone X with the 0.2% subtype. It hides zone D and unshaded zone X.
source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%'. The zone meanings paraphrase FEMA's Flood Zones glossary page (fema.gov/glossary/flood-zones, updated 8 July 2020) and FEMA's FloodSmart page 'What is my flood zone' (floodsmart.gov), both read on 4 October 2026. Those pages give FEMA's own wording. The FEMA service itself carries no definition table. Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
how_to_read: Read the letters as families. VE is the coastal high-hazard zone, where waves add force to flooding. A, A99, AE, AH and AO are the other 1% zones. X with the 0.2% subtype is outside the 1% area but inside the wider 0.2% area. Unshaded X and D are not drawn on the observatory's maps. FEMA gives base flood elevations or depths for some zones, but the observatory does not publish them: the file holds only the zone, subtype and SFHA flag.
caveats: A zone is a map category. It is not a flood depth, a forecast or a record of damage in a past storm.
Zone D means FEMA has not studied the area. It does not mean low risk.
Unshaded X means minimal hazard on FEMA's map, not no hazard. Heavy rain can flood land that FEMA maps as minimal hazard.
FEMA publishes an effective date for each map panel. The observatory does not keep it, so the age of a polygon cannot be read from this file.

values.A: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) where FEMA did not work out flood heights. Drawn on the maps. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 191 polygons.
values.A99: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) that a federal flood-control system under construction is meant to protect once it is finished. Drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon.
values.AE: 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) where FEMA gives base flood elevations, the height the 1% flood is expected to reach. It is the most common SFHA zone. Drawn on the maps; floodway polygons are drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1,760 polygons, 138 of them also marked floodway. Zone X has more polygons overall (2,368).
values.AH: 1% yearly chance shallow flooding area (SFHA), usually ponding about 1 to 3 feet deep, with base flood elevations. Drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 1 polygon.
values.AO: 1% yearly chance shallow flooding area (SFHA), usually water flowing over sloping ground about 1 to 3 feet deep, with flood depths given. Drawn; a floodway polygon is drawn red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 25 polygons, 1 also marked floodway.
values.VE: Coastal 1% yearly chance flood area (SFHA) with an added hazard from storm waves, with base flood elevations. Drawn in the darkest blue, except a river floodway polygon, which is red. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 539 polygons, 1 of them a river floodway inside the coastal zone.
values.X: Outside the 1% area and not part of the SFHA. It has two parts, set by ZONE_SUBTY: 0.2% annual chance flood hazard (drawn light blue) and area of minimal flood hazard (not drawn). In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,368 polygons, of which 1,648 are the 0.2% part and 720 the minimal-hazard part.
values.D: Possible but undetermined flood hazard: FEMA has not studied the area. Not part of the SFHA and not drawn. In the 2026-10 snapshot: 9 polygons.

example: A tourism place whose pin falls in an AE polygon is flagged as in a flood hazard area. A place in an X polygon with the 0.2% subtype is flagged as in a flood zone only.

name: FEMA flood zone subtype (ZONE_SUBTY)
plain: A second label from the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) that marks the 0.2% flood area, areas of minimal hazard and floodways. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is blank on 2,386 of the 4,894 polygons.
definition: ZONE_SUBTY refines FLD_ZONE in FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). It exists to separate the two kinds of zone X, which carry the same letter, and to mark floodways inside the 1% zones (the Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA). In the 2026-10 snapshot this file holds four values. The field is blank (stored as null) for 2,386 polygons: the 1% zones that are not floodways, plus zone D.
geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

method: Copied from NFHL layer 28 without change. The observatory reads a subtype that contains '0.2' as the 0.2% zone, and one that contains 'FLOODWAY' as a floodway, drawn red.
source_detail: FEMA NFHL MapServer layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), field ZONE_SUBTY. Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
how_to_read: Use the subtype to tell the two kinds of zone X apart. In the observatory, only zone X with the 0.2% subtype counts as a flood zone. Unshaded X is ignored.
caveats: The wording is FEMA's. It can change between FEMA releases, and a later release can add other values. Only these four occur in the 2026-10 snapshot.

The observatory counts a zone X polygon as a flood zone only when its subtype contains '0.2'. A zone X polygon with any other subtype would be hidden and not flagged, even if FEMA draws it as a hazard. Only two X subtypes occur in the 2026-10 snapshot.
Blank is not an error. It is the normal value for a 1% polygon that is not a floodway.

name: In the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF)
plain: A true or false flag on each polygon of the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) flood map. T means the polygon is in the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA), land with a 1% yearly chance of flooding, and F means it is not.
definition: SFHA_TF holds the letter T (true) or F (false). The Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) is the land FEMA maps as having a 1% chance of flooding in any year. T marks zones A, A99, AE, AH, AO and VE. F marks every zone X and zone D polygon. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2,517 polygons are T and 2,377 are F.
geography: Puerto Rico. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons. 77 of the 78 municipios overlap a polygon in the 1% or 0.2% zones. Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard). Coastal polygons extend over open water.

method: Copied without change from layer 28 of FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL). The build sets a place's sfha flag to yes when the place falls in a polygon where SFHA_TF is T.

Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.

The values are the text letters T and F, not true or false values.

name: FEMA flood zones (map layer)
plain: A map layer that shades the land the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as flood-prone: the 1% zones, floodways, coastal high-hazard zones and the 0.2% zone. Zone D and unshaded X are left blank.
definition: The layer called 'Flood zones' (source FEMA, from its National Flood Hazard Layer, NFHL) in the 2D map and in the 3D view draws the polygons of flood.geojson that are in the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) or are zone X with the 0.2% subtype. Red is a floodway. The darkest blue is a V zone (VE). Mid blue is any other SFHA zone (A, A99, AE, AH, AO). Light blue is the 0.2% zone. The layer hides zone D, unshaded X and the FEMA labels OPEN WATER and AREA NOT INCLUDED (neither occurs in the 2026-10 snapshot). Clicking a shaded area opens a popup with its zone and subtype, the same in the 2D map and the 3D view: one card with a section for each area under the click.
geography: In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 4,894 polygons for Puerto Rico. The layer draws 4,165 of them: 2,517 in the SFHA and 1,648 shaded zone X. It hides 729: 720 unshaded X and 9 zone D.

coverage.frequency: Retrieved from FEMA on 1 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The observatory keeps that copy until its next snapshot. FEMA changes its maps as new flood maps take effect, so a later copy can differ. 2026 is the year the observatory retrieved the layer, not the year FEMA drew each map. Map dates vary by panel and are not stored here.

method: Both maps draw the polygons in the SFHA and the zone X polygons whose subtype contains 0.2. They hide zone D, unshaded X and the two FEMA labels named above. Colours are red (floodway), darkest blue (V zones), mid blue (other SFHA zones) and light blue (0.2% zone), drawn at about 45% opacity. Place flags are not read from this file. They come from FEMA's unsimplified polygons.
source_detail: flood.geojson, built from FEMA NFHL layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones). Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
how_to_read: Colour shows the zone family, not depth. Use the zone letter and subtype to read what FEMA says. An unshaded area is not proof of safety. The layer 'Flood zones' covers the 1% zones and the 0.2% zone. In the place and municipality figures, 'in a flood hazard area' means the 1% area only (the Special Flood Hazard Area).
caveats: Drawn outlines are simplified to about 5 m. A place at a zone edge can look inside or outside on the map while its flag uses FEMA's unsimplified outline.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Florida municipio shows no flood colour because FEMA maps all of it as one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard), which the layer does not draw. The blank is a mapped result, not missing data. FEMA's panels for that municipio took effect between 2005 and 2009 (checked 5 October 2026).
Coastal polygons extend over open water. A shoreline place can sit in a VE zone.
The layer shows FEMA's mapped hazard, not sea level rise. The sea level layer of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is separate.

name: How flood exposure of a place is flagged
plain: The observatory flags a tourism place as in a flood hazard area when its map point lies inside an area that the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps with a 1% chance of flooding each year. A second, wider flag also covers the area FEMA maps with a 0.2% chance. Places in areas that FEMA marks as minimal hazard, or has not studied, get neither flag.
definition: For every place the build tests its coordinates against FEMA's flood polygons (point in polygon) and records two results. The sfha flag (Special Flood Hazard Area, SFHA) is yes when the point is inside a polygon where SFHA_TF is T. The flood zone value holds the zone and subtype when the point is in an SFHA polygon or in a zone X polygon with the 0.2% subtype. A point in unshaded X or zone D gets neither. If a point lies in more than one polygon, an SFHA polygon wins over a 0.2% polygon. Polygons labelled OPEN WATER or AREA NOT INCLUDED are skipped before testing (none occur in the 2026-10 snapshot).
unit: not applicable (yes or no per place)
geography: Every place in Puerto Rico's places file (32,541 listings in the 2026-10 snapshot). Municipality figures use the 24,209 counted places of that snapshot: tourism places with confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded (see 'Which places each municipality count includes').

coverage.frequency: Recalculated with each snapshot, from the FEMA copy retrieved on 1 October 2026.

method: The build tests each place's longitude and latitude with the 'within' test of Shapely (a Python geometry library) against FEMA's unsimplified polygons, not the simplified display file. A point exactly on an edge is not 'within'. Municipality counts use counted places only: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded. Percent in a flood hazard area is places in the SFHA divided by counted places, times 100, to one decimal.
source_detail: Overture Maps places; FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026.
how_to_read: 'In a flood hazard area' means the pin sits inside a polygon that FEMA maps with a 1% yearly chance of flooding. It does not say the place floods, how deep the water gets or whether the place has insurance.
caveats: Only the pin is tested. A building, beach or park can be partly inside a zone and partly outside.
The pin comes from Overture Maps and can be off the building by metres or more.
Coastal zones run along the shore, so shoreline places are flagged more often. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 428 of 817 counted beaches (52%) are in the SFHA, against 18% of all counted places.
No flag does not mean safe. Zone D and unshaded X are treated as not flagged, and FEMA's map covers only what FEMA studied.
Places of worship are flagged in the places file but left out of municipality percentages.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Florida municipio lies wholly inside one unshaded zone X polygon (minimal hazard), which is not flagged, so its 55 counted places show 0.0% in a flood hazard area. That is a mapped result, not missing data.
On a place, flood_zone X means the 0.2% zone. Unshaded X and zone D are never stored. A place with no flood_zone may still sit in unshaded X or outside FEMA's mapped area.
The percent is a share of listed places, not of land area, buildings or residents.
A municipio with few places can swing widely. See 'Tourism places in a flood hazard area (%)' for an example.
If a point sits in two polygons of the SFHA, the build keeps one of them and no rule decides which, so the zone letter can be either.

name: What FEMA flood zones can and cannot tell you
plain: Zones from the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) describe the mapped flood hazard at a point on the map. They do not give a building's elevation, a flood depth for a given storm, or a place's insurance status.
definition: A FEMA flood zone is a regulatory map category for an area. It says how FEMA classes the chance of flooding there. It does not say how high a building's floor is, how deep water will be in a given storm, or what insurance a place has. The observatory holds no insurance data, so it cannot say whether a place needs or has flood insurance.
geography: Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot

method: Applies to every FEMA-based figure in the observatory: the flood layers, a place's flood flag and the municipality percentages.
source_detail: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), layer 28 (Flood Hazard Zones). Cite as: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, Puerto Rico (DFIRM_ID beginning 72), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28, retrieved 1 October 2026 for observatory Snapshot 2026-10.
how_to_read: Treat the flags as a first screen. For a decision about a building, check the official FEMA flood map for that address and ask a qualified professional.
caveats: A 1% yearly chance is not 'once in 100 years'. Over 30 years the chance of at least one such flood is about 26%.
Zones come from studies of past and present conditions. They are not forecasts, and the observatory does not add sea level rise to them.
The flags are a point-in-polygon test on the pin (map point). They ignore ground elevation, drainage, flood-control works and building design.
FEMA's zones exist only where FEMA mapped. Zone D marks land that was not studied.

name: Sea level rise inundation layer (NOAA)
plain: Map tiles streamed live from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that show land that would be under water at high tide if the sea rose by 1 to 10 feet. The observatory does not store them.
definition: Each tile layer shows the area that NOAA's Office for Coastal Management maps as flooded when sea level is a set number of feet above today's mean higher high water (MHHW), the average height of the higher of the two daily high tides. The observatory offers whole-foot steps from 1 to 10 ft. NOAA draws the tiles. The browser asks coast.noaa.gov for them while the layer is on. No sea level data are kept in the observatory's data files.
unit: feet above mean higher high water (MHHW)
geography: Puerto Rico coast, as covered by NOAA's national layers

coverage.frequency: Live from NOAA each time the layer is shown

method: NOAA draws the tiles. While the layer is on, the browser asks https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr/slr_{N}ft/MapServer for tiles, where N is the height in feet. Tiles are requested up to zoom level 16 and enlarged beyond that. If NOAA does not answer, the page shows a message. For the controls, see 'Sea level rise switch and slider (2D map)', '3D view: Sea level by year' and '3D view: flood zones and sea level switches'.
source_detail: NOAA Office for Coastal Management, Sea Level Rise Viewer, ArcGIS service dc_slr, tile layers slr_1ft to slr_10ft (https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr). The tiles are streamed live, so there is no retrieval date to give: cite the feet value and the date you viewed the layer.
how_to_read: Tinted areas are where NOAA maps flooding at the chosen height above mean higher high water, at the highest regular high tides. It is a what-if for planning, not a forecast for a year. NOAA says all features should be verified with a site visit. To cite a layer, give the feet value and the date you viewed it, because NOAA can update the service.
caveats: NOAA describes the layers as a screening-level tool. They show the scale of possible flooding, not exact locations.
NOAA says the layers do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction.
NOAA says the layers show water at the highest high tides and exclude wind-driven tides. Its viewer does not model storm surge.

As of 4 October 2026, NOAA's service for the 3 ft layer holds two sublayers, 'Low-lying Areas' and 'Depth', and the observatory shows NOAA's full tile set. NOAA's Sea Level Rise Viewer help explains how NOAA defines low-lying areas. Read it before concluding that a particular place would flood.
NOAA provides the data as is, for planning and not for permits or navigation.
The observatory keeps no copy. If NOAA changes or removes the service, the layer stops working.

name: Landslide susceptibility layer (USGS)
plain: A map from the US Geological Survey of how likely the ground is to slide when intense rain falls, in five classes from low to extremely high. The tiles are streamed live; the observatory does not store them.
definition: The USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (Hughes and Schulz, 2020), drawn on the 2D map and draped on the terrain of the 3D view in its five classes: Low (the least susceptible 40% of the main island), Moderate (the next 30%), High (20%), Very High (9%) and Extremely High (the top 1%). The browser asks the first author's tile copy for the tiles while the layer is on; nothing is stored in the observatory's data files.
geography: The main island of Puerto Rico (not Vieques or Culebra)

coverage.frequency: Streamed from the map service each time the layer is shown; the model itself is static (2020).

method: While the layer is on, the browser asks https://tiles.arcgis.com/tiles/TQ9qkk0dURXSP7LQ/arcgis/rest/services/Susceptibilidad_Derrumbe_PR/MapServer for tiles up to zoom 17 and enlarges them beyond that, at 60% opacity, under the Soils layer. The same tiles are what landslide.py reads for the barrio and municipio figures, checked there against the report (see landslide.ls_land_high_pct).
source_detail: Hughes and Schulz (2020), USGS Open-File Report 2020-1022; GIS layer: https://doi.org/10.5066/P990ZP4C. Tiles: https://tiles.arcgis.com/tiles/TQ9qkk0dURXSP7LQ/arcgis/rest/services/Susceptibilidad_Derrumbe_PR/MapServer.
how_to_read: The redder the area, the more likely a landslide is there when intense rain falls; the blue-violet class is the most susceptible 1% of the island. It shows where a slide is more likely, not when or whether one will happen. Turn it on with the Soils layer's slope to compare.
caveats: The authors say the map is for planning and emergency preparation and is not a substitute for a site-specific slope-stability study.
It does not show where a landslide travels downhill, and deep bedrock landslides and earthquake-triggered ones are poorly represented.
Vieques and Culebra are not in the map.
The layer needs the map service to answer; if the copy is moved or removed, the layer stops working.

name: Sea level rise by year and scenario (3D view)
plain: The 3D view picks a layer of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) from a year and a scenario. It reads the scenario's rise in metres for that year, converts it to feet, rounds to a whole foot and keeps it between 1 and 10.
definition: In the Time tab of the 3D view, you choose a year (2020 to 2150, in steps of 5) and one of four NOAA 2022 scenarios. The page holds a small table of global mean sea level rise, in metres above the year-2000 level, for 2020, 2050, 2100 and 2150 in each scenario. It joins those points with straight lines, multiplies the metres by 3.28084 to get feet, rounds to the nearest whole foot and limits the result to 1 to 10 ft. It then loads NOAA's layer for that number of feet.
unit: feet of sea level rise (whole feet, 1 to 10)
geography: Global mean curves applied to Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: Fixed in the page code. It changes only when the code changes.

method: For a year y between two table years y0 and y1, the page works out: metres = m0 + (m1 - m0) x (y - y0) / (y1 - y0). Feet = metres x 3.28084, rounded half up, then at least 1 and at most 10. The 2D map has no year. Its slider sets the feet directly.
source_detail: Sweet et al. (2022), Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for the United States: Updated Mean Projections and Extreme Water Level Probabilities Along U.S. Coastlines, NOAA Technical Report NOS 01, for the curves; NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer for the layers. The observatory's values are approximate readings of the report's tables, not NOAA's published numbers.
how_to_read: Several years show the same layer, because the result is rounded to whole feet. The layer is 1 ft from 2020 until 2050 in High and Intermediate-High, until 2060 in Intermediate and until 2090 in Intermediate-Low. A year on the slider is a position on a scenario curve, not a prediction that the sea will reach that level in that year. The Year slider opens at 2050 and the scenario at Intermediate, which gives the 1 ft layer.
caveats: The curves are global averages typed into the page code. They are not Puerto Rico local values.
The scenarios measure rise above the year-2000 sea level. The NOAA layers show water above today's mean higher high water. The observatory treats the two as the same number of feet.
Only four scenarios are offered: Intermediate-Low, Intermediate, Intermediate-High and High. NOAA's 2022 report also has a Low scenario, which the observatory does not offer.
The result is capped at 10 ft, so the High scenario in 2150 (12.8 ft) shows the 10 ft layer.

The layer is never lower than 1 ft. In 2020 the table value is 0.07 m (0.2 ft) in every scenario, so the 1 ft layer shows more water than the table gives. The floor changes the result only while the table value is under 0.5 ft: up to 2025 in High and Intermediate-High, and up to 2030 in Intermediate and Intermediate-Low.
These metres are the observatory's own approximate readings of NOAA's tables, not NOAA's published numbers. For scenario values to cite, use the NOAA report.

name: How storms near Puerto Rico are selected
plain: The observatory keeps every Atlantic storm from 1851 to 2025 that had a recorded position within 250 km (155 miles) of the centre of Puerto Rico. The storms come from the Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). In the 2026-10 snapshot that is 157 storms.
definition: The National Hurricane Center (NHC), part of NOAA, publishes HURDAT2, the Atlantic hurricane database: a list of storms, each with positions and winds every 6 hours. The build measures the distance from each best-track position to a fixed point at 18.22 N, 66.45 W, near the middle of the main island. A storm is kept when its closest position is 250 km (about 155 miles) or less from that point. Each kept storm carries four derived values: min_dist_km, max_wind, wind_near_pr and cat_near_pr.
geography: Atlantic storms with a best-track position within 250 km of the centre of Puerto Rico (157 storms in the 2026-10 snapshot)

coverage.frequency: The observatory uses NOAA's release file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The build looks up the newest NOAA file only when it is run with the refresh option; it does not check on its own. NOAA adds each season after it ends and may revise earlier seasons.

method: 1) Read the HURDAT2 Atlantic file (hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt): one header line per storm (id, name), then one row per position (date, time, status, latitude, longitude, wind in knots). 2) Keep every row of a kept storm as its track, so the track covers the storm's whole life. 3) min_dist_km is the smallest great-circle (haversine) distance from any position to the centre point, rounded to a whole km. Keep the storm when the unrounded value is 250 km or less. 4) max_wind is the largest wind on the whole track. 5) wind_near_pr is the largest wind among positions within 250 km of the centre point. 6) cat_near_pr is the Saffir-Simpson category of wind_near_pr, with 0 for winds below 64 knots. 7) Sort storms by the time of their first position. meta.json records the count and the year range.
source_detail: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
how_to_read: 250 km is measured from one point, not from the coast. Along the compass lines through that point, the circle reaches about 160 km beyond the east coast, 175 km beyond the west coast and 220 km beyond the north and south coasts. A storm on the list may never have touched land.
caveats: The test uses best-track positions, not the line between them. A fast storm could cross the circle between two positions and be left out.
Only Atlantic storms (id prefix AL) are read. Eastern Pacific storms are not included.

Observation methods changed a great deal between 1851 and 2025. Older tracks and winds are less certain, so counts by decade should not be read as a trend. In the 2026-10 snapshot the 2020s have six years (2020 to 2025), so that decade is incomplete.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 157 storms are kept, and 65 had hurricane-strength wind (category 1 or higher) near the island by this method.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 157 include 6 systems that were only a low, disturbance or tropical wave when within 250 km, and 22 storms with a single position inside the circle. The count is storms that came near, not storms that struck the island.

name: Limits of the hurricane data (HURDAT2 best tracks)
plain: The Hurricane Database, 2nd generation (HURDAT2) of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is a best-track record. It is revised after each season, shows the storm's own wind and position, and says nothing about rain, surge, damage or deaths.
definition: A best track is a final estimate of a storm's position and wind. National Hurricane Center (NHC) specialists build it after the season ends, from all the observations. NHC revises it after each season and sometimes re-analyses older storms. The observatory uses one release, covering 1851 to 2025. A newer release is used only when the observatory is rebuilt to use it.
geography: Atlantic basin, storms within 250 km of Puerto Rico

coverage.frequency: The observatory uses NOAA's release file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). The build looks up the newest NOAA file only when it is run with the refresh option; it does not check on its own. NOAA adds each season after it ends and may revise earlier seasons.

method: Applies to every storm value in the observatory: id, name, year, track, max_wind, wind_near_pr, cat_near_pr and min_dist_km.
source_detail: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Hurricane Center (NHC), HURDAT2 Atlantic best-track database 1851-2025, file hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt, https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/#hurdat, retrieved 5 October 2026. Format reference: Landsea and Franklin (2013), Atlantic Hurricane Database Uncertainty and Presentation of a New Database Format, Monthly Weather Review 141, 3576-3592.
how_to_read: Use the data to see which storms came near the island and how strong they were while near. Do not use it to say how much damage a storm did.
caveats: The file runs through the 2025 season (NHC file updated 23 September 2026). Storms after the 2025 season are not in the 2026-10 snapshot. NHC also revised some 1971 to 1975 storms in that file, so a few older values differ from earlier snapshots (for example, Eloise 1975 now peaks at 55 knots near the island, so it is category 0, not 1).
HURDAT2 holds no rainfall, storm surge, damage or death figures. The observatory keeps only time, position, wind and status. It drops central pressure and wind-radius columns.
Winds are sustained one-minute averages in 5-knot steps. They are not gusts.
Older storms are less certain, and some storms may be missing from the early record.
Storm names repeat. Use the id.

name: Protection level, GAP status (GAP_Sts)
plain: A code from 1 to 4 that shows how strongly an area is managed to protect nature. Codes 1 and 2 are managed for biodiversity. Code 3 may allow uses such as mining or logging. Code 4 has no known requirement to protect biodiversity.
definition: GAP_Sts is the status code of the Gap Analysis Project (GAP) of the US Geological Survey, as carried in the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US). It sorts areas by how they are managed for biodiversity. In the 2026-10 snapshot the counts are: code 4, 440; code 2, 181; code 1, 25; code 3, 19. The values are text digits.

method: Copied from PAD-US without change. When a place sits in several protected areas, the build keeps the one with the strictest (lowest) GAP status.

caveats: The status describes how land is managed on paper. It does not measure habitat condition.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 59% of the counted places flagged as in a protected area are in GAP 4 land (509 of 869).

name: How a place is flagged as inside a protected area
plain: A tourism place counts as inside a protected area when its map point falls in a polygon (map shape) of the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) other than a proclamation outline. If it falls in several, the strictest Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status is kept.
definition: For every place the build tests its coordinates against the PAD-US polygons. Records with designation PROC (outlines) are skipped. If the point is in more than one other record, the record with the lowest GAP status wins. The place then carries that record's name (protected_area) and GAP status (protected_gap).
unit: not applicable (yes or no per place)
geography: Every place in Puerto Rico's places file. In the 2026-10 snapshot, municipality counts use the 24,209 counted places (tourism places with confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded).

coverage.frequency: Recalculated with each snapshot, from the PAD-US copy retrieved on 1 October 2026.

method: The build tests each place with the Shapely 'within' test against the unsimplified PAD-US polygons. Municipality counts (in_protected) use counted places only: confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship excluded.

In the same snapshot, one 'Unknown Local Park' record that spans the island holds 117 of the flagged places.
Only the pin is tested. The pin can be off the building.
If two records share the lowest GAP status, the build keeps one of them and no rule chooses which. The protected_area name can be either.
